transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, it's good to meet you too. Um, so, what brings me in... well, it's mostly work stuff, honestly. I'm a supervisor for a sales team, and lately—well, maybe not just lately, but it's really starting to become a problem—I just keep making these incredibly dumb mistakes on my sales reports. And it's so frustrating because I know how to do them, I've done them a million times, but I'll be pulling data from the team dashboard, and I'll just straight-up copy the wrong numbers. Like, I'll put a 7 instead of a 9, or I'll put a guy's numbers in the wrong column, and it throws the whole spreadsheet off. 

And it's not just the numbers, either. We have these procedures I have to check off, making sure the team followed all the steps for a big client account, and I'll just completely miss a line. I'll skip right over it. The crazy part is, I always check my work. I swear I do. I'll sit there, look over the whole document, think to myself, "Yep, looks good, everything is perfect," and then my boss will call me in the next day and point out that I missed an entire section or messed up the final tally. It makes me look like I don't care, or like I'm not paying attention, but I am trying to pay attention! It's just like my brain just blips over the details, no matter how hard I try to focus on them. It’s getting to the point where I'm second-guessing everything I do, and it's just exhausting.
When you were a child, did you also often make careless mistakes or have trouble paying close attention to details?

Yeah, actually, I was totally like this as a kid, too. It’s funny you ask that, because my mom, she still brings it up. Like, she’ll joke about it at family dinners, which is... you know, a little annoying, but she’s not wrong. She kept all these old report cards and notes from my teachers in elementary school. I remember this one teacher, Mrs. Gable in third grade, she used to send notes home constantly. And they all basically said the exact same thing. It was always, "He rushes through his assignments," or "He doesn't check his work." I'd finish a worksheet in five minutes and just turn it in without even looking at it twice, and of course, half the answers would be wrong because I just didn't read the questions right.

And it wasn't just the careless mistakes, either. The notes were always about how I'd lose my homework. Like, I'd do the homework, I knew I did it, but by the time I got to school, it was just... gone. Vanished into the black hole of my backpack, or I left it on the kitchen counter. And the teachers were always writing about how I talked out of turn. I'd just blurt things out in the middle of a lesson because a thought popped into my head and I felt like I had to say it right then and there. Plus, they were always having to remind me to stay in my seat. I couldn't just sit still at my desk. I'd be up sharpening my pencil, or going to the trash can, or just wandering over to talk to a friend. So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing. It’s like the same exact stuff I’m doing now with my sales reports, just... you know, the adult version of it, I guess. It's always been there, just this constant struggle to slow down and actually look at the details.
As an adult, do you often feel restless or have a hard time staying seated when you’re expected to remain in one place?

Oh, yeah, absolutely. It's actually a huge issue for me, especially with my job. We have these weekly sales meetings, right? And they're not even that long, maybe an hour, sometimes an hour and a half if the regional director is in town. But for me, it feels like an eternity. I’ll sit down in the conference room—and I always try to pick a chair near the door, just in case—and for the first ten minutes, I'm okay. But then, it's like this... this physical sensation starts creeping up. Sitting through a long meeting feels like my body is buzzing inside. It's hard to explain, but it's like my nerves are vibrating and my muscles are just screaming at me to move. 

I literally cannot just sit still and listen. I have to shift around in my chair, cross my legs, uncross them, lean forward, lean back. I'll start tapping my foot, and I try to do it quietly so I don't annoy the people next to me, but sometimes I don't even realize I'm doing it until someone gives me a look. And if the meeting goes on too long, I just can't take it anymore. I have to make an excuse to get up. I'll pretend I need to use the restroom, or I'll grab my empty coffee mug and act like I desperately need a refill right that second, or I'll even pretend my phone buzzed with an urgent client text just so I can step out into the hallway and walk around for a minute. It's embarrassing, honestly, because I'm a supervisor, I should be setting an example, right? I should be locked in, taking notes, nodding along. But instead, I'm just sitting there fighting my own body, trying to ignore this overwhelming urge to just stand up and pace around the room. It’s like that buzzing feeling just builds and builds until I have to do something about it.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports ADHD, combined presentation: persistent symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity are present in adulthood and were clearly established in childhood, with functional impairment at work. Inattention is shown by repeated careless mistakes, missing steps, and poor detail checking; hyperactivity/impulsivity is shown by inability to remain seated, internal restlessness, fidgeting, blurting out, and wandering from seat as a child. Symptoms are chronic rather than situational.
